questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The 1674 edition of Paradise Lost: books and prose summaries
questions.learningObjective: read a change in a book's division as a change in the equipment it gives a reader
questions.stem: Milton's Paradise Lost was first printed in 1667 divided into ten books and with no prose summaries. The 1674 printing divided the same poem into twelve books and prefixed a short prose account of events to each. What does the change of 1674 tell a reader about the kind of text its editors believed they had in hand?

options.text: That they expected readers who would need carrying, since the summaries let a reader hold the plot without keeping the whole of a very long poem in mind
That the poem had been rewritten, since a change in the number of books can only be produced by composing fresh lines between the new divisions
options.misconception: assumes that dividing a poem into more books requires rewriting, when the 1674 change split the existing text and nothing more

options.text: That the poem had been translated, since a text arranged as twelve books must be answering a twelve-book original in some other language
options.misconception: infers a foreign original from the number of books, which records an arrangement and not a source language

options.text: That the poem was in manuscript before 1667, since a printed text needing summaries cannot also be an author's own fair copy
options.misconception: contrasts print and manuscript as if summaries were impossible in a fair copy, which is a non-sequitur about materials

questions.explanation: The useful thing to notice is what the summaries are for. A poem of this length, unrhymed, with no precedent among Latin or Greek epics for a creation story, gives a reader no external shape to hold on to; Virgil's reader at least knew roughly where the ships would be. Prefixing a short prose account to each book hands the reader a way of keeping the whole in view without holding it all at once, and the twelve-book division, which brings the poem into line with the twelve books of the Aeneid, was made at the same time. The summaries are the clue that the editors had decided the poem needed navigation rather than assumed it. The first option turns a division into a rewriting, which the book's own history contradicts: the poem's lines were not newly composed. The third infers translation from an arrangement, and the fourth sets print against manuscript as if one material excluded summaries and the other did not, which was never the case for either.
questions.hint: Ask what a prose summary offers that a division into books does not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The 1668 additions defending Paradise Lost's unrhymed measure
questions.learningObjective: explain what an author's added note commits him to about a poem's form
questions.stem: When Paradise Lost was reissued in 1668, sixteen pages of new front matter were added: a note from the printer, a page of errata, and a short defence of the poem's unrhymed measure in which Milton ranks rhyme as an invention of a barbarous age. What has Milton committed himself to by writing that defence into the book?

options.text: That the poem is prose with line breaks, since a defence of unrhymed measure is only ever an admission that the lines are not verse
options.misconception: takes a claim about rhyme for a claim about verse itself, which is the opposite of what the note argues

options.text: That the poem's form is a deliberate, defensible position he means to be held to, since a stated rule about rhyme is a claim a later reader can use against him
That the poem's metre is a private experiment he expects readers to forgive, since defending a choice is the same as admitting it needed defence
options.misconception: assumes that arguing a case for a form amounts to apologising for it, which reverses the purpose of the note

options.text: That the printer asked for the note, so Milton's opinion of his own verse is not really Milton's opinion at all
options.misconception: shifts responsibility to the printer and dismisses the note as a bookseller's device

questions.explanation: A note is a claim laid on the table, and this one is laid deliberately. By ranking rhyme as a late invention serving poor matter and worse metre, and by placing his measure in the lineage of Homer and Virgil, Milton converts a technical observation about the page into a position somebody could argue with. That is the cost of writing the defence down: the rule gives a reader a standard, and a later writer who breaks it can be measured against it. The printer's presence in the matter does not soften this, since the note is in Milton's own name and his argument is not the printer's. The first option misreads the whole point, because defending a verse form as a deliberate choice is the opposite of calling it prose. The second treats argument as apology, which is a modern error about how authors write prefaces. The third reduces authorship by attributing an argument to whoever happened to print it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader gains the right to do once a rule has been stated in print.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Milton's own numbering of his sonnets against the printed numbering
questions.learningObjective: handle a disagreement in a text's numbering as evidence rather than error
questions.stem: The sonnet beginning with the poet's account of his light being spent is numbered 19 in the numbering Milton himself used in his notebook of poems, and 16 in the printed collection. Two numbers circulate in print and neither is a misprint. What follows for a reader who wants to cite the poem?

options.text: That the lower number is the true one, since a printed book outranks a working notebook whenever the two disagree
options.misconception: ranks print above manuscript as a general rule, which settles the question by a habit rather than by evidence

options.text: That the number matters little either way, so a reader may use whichever figure is nearest to hand without troubling to name the edition
options.misconception: treats a citation as a matter of convenience, when a number identifies a particular arrangement of a particular collection

options.text: That the poem should be cited by its first words or by a name for it, and the number given with the source, because the two numbers come from two different acts of ordering
That one of the two numbers must be an error, so a reader should assume a copying mistake until a copy of the source is produced
options.misconception: assumes a divergence is always a mistake, which is the assumption the two acts of ordering make impossible

questions.explanation: The divergence is not a mistake in either place, which is exactly why it has to be reported rather than tidied away. Milton's manuscript notebook carried one arrangement of the sonnets, the one he had made while writing them; the printed collection numbered them in a different order, following the sequence of the book. Two acts of ordering, two numberings, both correct within their own system. The consequence for a reader is practical: a bare number tells a reader nothing, because the number means different things in the two systems, and a number quoted without its source is a number that cannot be checked. The second option offers a rule, and the rule is wrong, since a printed edition is a later decision about sequence rather than a record of the earlier one. The third treats a reference as decoration. The fourth mistakes a documented difference for an error, and would have a reader reject a discrepancy that is itself the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what a number means when two orderings both number the same poem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The 1638 memorial volume in which Lycidas appeared
questions.learningObjective: place a poem in the printing context that shaped how its readers met it
questions.stem: Lycidas was printed in 1638 in a short volume of elegies assembled to commemorate a young Cambridge man drowned crossing the Irish Sea, and most of the other poems in the volume were written in Latin or Greek. What does that context do to a reader approaching Milton's poem for the first time?

options.text: It makes the poem read as an exercise in a university exercise book, since sharing a volume with Latin verses puts it in the same category as the rest
options.misconception: reduces a memorial volume to a university exercise book, which the volume's purpose for the bereaved contradicts

options.text: It explains why the poem's own title page is in Latin, since a volume whose title is Latin would naturally carry English poems inside it
options.misconception: supposes the language of a title page determines the language of the contents, which is not how a volume is arranged

options.text: It makes the English poem the odd one out in a way that argues against reading it at all, since a reader should hold back from a volume in five languages
options.misconception: treats the presence of Greek and Latin as a reason to decline the English poem, when the volume was assembled to be read

options.text: It tells the reader that this is a contribution to a shared act of mourning, and that its Greek and Latin neighbours set the expectations the English poem answers

questions.explanation: A poem is read differently when the reader knows what it was written to do and for whom. Lycidas was one contribution to a volume commissioned by a university community to mark a death, and it was the only English poem of consequence among contributions in Latin and Greek. That tells a reader the expected shape of what follows: a lament in the classical manner, formal, bounded, written by a person of comparable education to the one mourned. The context therefore supplies the register the poem works in and the occasion it is answering, which is why the poem can be about something other than the dead man and still be a proper part of a volume of elegies. The first option misdescribes the volume as a collection of exercises, when the fact that relatives and college members contributed to it makes that implausible. The second confuses a title page with a contents list. The fourth makes a multilingual volume a reason to decline, which reverses the point of assembling one.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader expects of a poem written among other people's elegies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The turn in Lycidas from private grief to public complaint
questions.learningObjective: locate a shift of register and name what the shift changes
questions.stem: For its first half Lycidas mourns a drowned friend in the personified countryside, and then the poem turns: the nymphs who should have saved him are scolded for looking away, and the shepherd figure is imagined as a man who spends his life in the same district and cannot leave it. What has the poem gained by making that turn?

options.text: An ending, since a poem that begins in grief can only close by becoming an argument, and the change of subject is the mechanism by which it ends
options.misconception: treats a turn of argument as a structural necessity of any poem that moves from feeling to reasoning

options.text: A second subject in the same figure, so the private dead man and the public complaint are two uses of one image and the poem's argument is doubled rather than left
A correction of the first half, so that the pastoral opening is shown to have been a mistake the later stanzas take back
options.misconception: reads the turn as a repudiation of the opening, when the two halves sustain each other

options.text: A distraction, since a reader who has been asked to mourn one person is now being asked to think about a whole profession and has been led off the subject
options.misconception: treats widening a subject as losing it, which is the ordinary way a public lyric works

questions.explanation: The turn is not a change of subject so much as a change in what the same figure is for. The nymphs, the shepherd and the district that keeps a man in place are all still there, but they have been turned outward: the death that ended at the river now becomes an instance of a grievance about how the living are employed and confined. Because the second use of the figure depends on the first, the reader arrives at the public claim already inside a picture of what confinement costs, and the claim is made in the vocabulary of loss rather than in the vocabulary of argument. That is what the poem gains. The second option makes a turn into a mechanical necessity, when a poem that stayed in grief for its whole length would have been perfectly shaped. The third supposes the poem repudiates its own opening, and nothing in the later stanzas withdraws the earlier ones. The fourth treats widening as loss of subject, which is the standard way a lyric moves from a person to a condition.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two halves need each other or merely succeed each other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Conventions of the pastoral elegy that Lycidas works inside
questions.learningObjective: separate the conventions a poem uses from the claims it makes in them
questions.stem: A reader lists four features of a poem about a shepherd lost at sea. Three of them are conventions the genre supplies ready-made, and one is a particular decision this poem makes. Which three belong to the convention rather than to the individual poem?

options.text: The dead man is given a Greek shepherd's name so that the poem can treat him inside a pastoral world rather than as a named contemporary
The poem opens by breaking into a familiar invocation, the formal signal that a lament proper is beginning
The poem refuses the consolations of the genre and ends on the claim that poetic fame is not a plant that grows on ordinary soil
The poem closes by abandoning the shepherds altogether and turning to the reader in the poet's own voice
options.misconception: mistakes a move the poem makes for a move the genre supplies, which is exactly where the individual choice begins

questions.explanation: A convention is a decision the genre has already made available, so recognising it tells a reader where the poet's own choices begin. The Greek shepherd's name is one: it converts a dead contemporary into a figure the pastoral convention can handle, and every elegy that wants the convention has to make that move. The formal invocation at the opening is another, a signal so standard that a poem using it is announcing that it is now doing the thing it was written to do. So is the refusal of consolation, since the closing claim about fame and immortality is a stock pivot of the pastoral elegy and poets turn it in every direction. What is not convention is the poem's own handling of the shepherds at the end, where the convention is dropped while the first person remains. The point of the distinction is practical: conventions are the ground on which a reading stands, and an argument that praises or faults a poem for using one has confused the ground with the building.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four would also be true of a different elegy in the genre.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Jonson's Epigram 22 and the combination of epitaph and inventory
questions.learningObjective: identify the tonal seam inside a short commemorative poem
questions.stem: Ben Jonson's Epigram 22, printed in 1636, is an elegy for his own daughter who died in her first year. It opens by stating what is laid in the grave, and then it goes on to list the gifts that visitors bring to a small child's tomb. What does the list do to the poem?

options.text: It places the poem's claim in tension with its occasions, since a grave gets fowls and fruit for a year and then only stones, and the poem counts what is left behind
It removes the poem from grief entirely, since a catalogue of offerings is what a formal epitaph contains and no personal feeling survives inside one
options.misconception: assumes a formal element excludes feeling, which is the assumption a tonal seam exists to defeat

options.text: It shows that the poem is a satire on mourners rather than a lament, since naming the gifts is the same as mocking the people who bring them
options.misconception: reads the inventory as an attack on visitors, when the pressure comes from the passage of time

options.text: It supplies the missing argument of the elegy, since a father's grief needs a cause and a basket of pears is a better cause than a death
options.misconception: supplies a causal argument where the poem offers an observation about what survives

questions.explanation: The seam is the point. An epitaph states a fact and holds still; an inventory of offerings is exact, particular and time-bound, and it draws attention to how much of a life is represented by objects that visitors bring and then stop bringing. Set side by side, the two kinds of statement measure the same grave by two clocks, one belonging to the person who died and one to the people who come afterwards. A reader who wants to know what the poem is doing should notice that it never says the loss is bearable, and never says it is not; it says what happens in the year after, and the reader supplies the rest. The first option mistakes a formal element for the absence of feeling, which is the very effect the seam produces. The third converts a measured observation into an attack on the living, which the poem nowhere makes. The fourth is the tempting error, because a list does look like an argument, but the list argues about duration rather than about cause.
questions.hint: Ask how the two passages in the poem measure time differently.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The court masque as a performance record rather than a page
questions.learningObjective: read a performed work's calendar against the printed text
questions.stem: Ben Jonson's masque Oberon, the Faery Prince was performed at Whitehall on 1 January 1611, with the prince of Wales dancing the title part, and it was the sixth of the expensive court shows Jonson and Inigo Jones had staged since 1605. What does that record tell a reader who only has the printed masque?

options.text: That the printed masque is a transcript of what the court saw, so a reader can treat the text as a complete record of the evening
options.misconception: assumes the printed text is a transcript, when a masque is written to be staged with machines and dancers

options.text: That the masque's scale and cost are the reason the text was printed at all, since a private performance leaves otherwise no trace
options.misconception: makes printing a consequence of expense, when a performance could be written for and then simply performed

options.text: That the text was revised for print into a reading poem, so the book version and the performed version should be assumed to differ substantially
options.misconception: asserts a substantial difference between stage text and printed text, which the survival of both does not show

options.text: That the dance and the scenery were written into the text itself, so a reader of the printed masque can see the whole shape of the evening
options.misconception: supposes the printed words include the choreography and the machinery, which were separate commissions

questions.explanation: A masque is a score for a building full of people and machines, and its meaning in performance comes heavily from what the words do not contain: the dancers, the scenes, the music, the engineering. Knowing that the work was staged at court on a known date, with a known dancer in the title part, at great expense, tells a reader that the printed text is one component of a much larger occasion and that the components were separately made. It also tells a reader that the text and the performance had separate fates, and that the text available now is the text as printed, not a record of the evening. What the record does not do is let a reader reconstruct the performance from the page, which is the trap in the first and third options: nobody watching the dance would have inferred the choreography from the printed dialogue. The second option mistakes expense for a printing motive.
questions.hint: Ask what parts of a court masque were not the poet's work at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two different poems both addressed to Celia
questions.learningObjective: distinguish two works that share a title and an addressee
questions.stem: Two short love poems by Ben Jonson share a title of the form Song to Celia and both appeared in his 1616 collection. One opens by proposing to drink to the beloved with nothing but the eyes, and the other opens by proposing to prove the sports of love while the lovers still can. What is the practical consequence of the shared title?

options.text: That the two are alternate versions of one poem, so a reader should treat the differences as late revisions of a single text
options.misconception: collapses two distinct poems into one on the strength of a shared title

options.text: That the collection's compiler made an error, since a volume of one poet's poems should not carry two titles in the same form
options.misconception: supposes the shared title is a printing error rather than a habit of the collection

options.text: That the later poem is a parody of the earlier, since only a writer imitating another would reuse so exact a title
options.misconception: assumes reuse of a title proves parody, when a poet addressing the same woman reuses a plain form of words

options.text: That a reader must give the title plus enough of the opening to fix which poem is meant, since the collection printed both and the title alone does not

questions.explanation: Shared titles are a normal feature of a verse collection and a standing hazard for anyone citing from it. Here the two poems are entirely separate works, different in argument, in metre and in what they ask of the reader: one turns the toast into a claim about the eye and the glass, the other turns it into a claim about time and the moment. Nothing in either indicates revision of the other, and there is no tradition of the second answering the first. What the situation requires is a fuller reference, and a good reference is short: the title with the opening words, or a line from inside the poem, fixes the identity at once. The first option is the expensive error, because a reader who merges the poems will quote from one while citing the other, which is the kind of error that survives into print for decades. The third and fourth both invent a cause where the evidence supports only a naming problem.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must add to a title in order to name a poem unambiguously.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Temple, 1633, and the machinery that put it in print
questions.learningObjective: read a volume's printing history as part of its authorship
questions.stem: George Herbert's The Temple was printed at Cambridge in 1633, within months of his death, with a preface presenting him as a model priest, and a second edition of the same year added further matter. What does that sequence tell a reader about who shaped the volume?

options.text: That the book's public image was in part a gift of its editors, since a preface describing the author's exemplary life can only have been written by someone who admired him
That the poems were written to a plan the author completed before printing, so the preface can be taken as a statement of his own intentions
options.misconception: supposes an author wrote his own afterlife in advance, which the date of the printing forbids

options.text: That the second edition proves the first was misprinted, since publishers do not reprint a book they have got right
options.misconception: treats a second edition as a correction, when it is a revision

options.text: That the volume was written for print from the start, since a book printed within a year of the author's death must have been prepared for readers
options.misconception: infers intention to publish from the speed of the printing, which shows the opposite

questions.explanation: A book that appears within months of its author's death has had to be assembled by somebody else, and the assembly is visible on the page. The preface that presents Herbert as a modest and exemplary clergyman was not written by a man who had already surveyed his own reputation; it is the work of a friend and editor, and it does a specific job, which is to make the poems readable as the life of a saint as well as the poems of a writer. A reader who wants to know what the poetry is doing should therefore hold two things apart: the poems, and the account of the man that the book's front matter supplies. The second edition of the same year shows the shaping was still in progress. The first option is impossible on the chronology, since the author was dead. The third misreads revision as error. The fourth is the subtlest wrong turn: a book printed at once after a death is evidence of a plan not to publish, not of a plan to publish.
questions.hint: Ask who could have written the preface, given the date of the printing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Herbert's curtal sonnet and the punctuation that serves as a stave
questions.learningObjective: read a shortening of the line as a claim about what a unit of verse is

stimulus.body: an original curtal sonnet written for this question in Herbert's manner, printed in the stem
stimulus.license: original text written for this question; no protected text used

questions.stem: A passage written for this question in the manner of Herbert's Easter Wings runs: "Lord, who hast made the first of men, / Though he hath lost the same, / And now decayeth more and more, / Till he became / Most plain: / With thee / O let me rise / As larks, at break of day, / And sing this day thy victories: / Then shall the fall lift up my flight." Each printed line is cut into two by its own punctuation, and each half is a complete foot. What is the convention doing?

options.text: Shortening the poem so that it can be memorised, since a shorter line takes less breath and a singer can therefore fit more of it into one tune
options.misconception: explains a formal device by a practical convenience in singing, which the printed page does not support

options.text: Making the line a container to be divided, so the shape of the stanza on the page is itself part of the argument about a body that is broken and remade
Imitating the shape of a pair of wings, so that the reader's eye travels out and back across each line in the manner of a bird's flight
options.misconception: takes the poem's title for its structural principle when the structure is independent of the title

options.text: Avoiding a rhyme the poet could not find, which is why the lines end without rhyme in the ordinary places
options.misconception: reads a formal pattern as a failure to find rhymes, when the pattern is regular and repeated

questions.explanation: Two ten-line stanzas of ten lines each, every line cut in two by a mark that does the work of a bar of music, gives twenty short units where a sonnet expects fourteen long ones. Nothing in the metre is broken; the lines have been shortened and then re-joined, and the reader is asked to hear two beats where there was one. What that does is to make the printed page a diagram. A sonnet of this kind is about a soul that is decayed and remade, and the page it is printed on is a figure of exactly that operation, cut in half and held together by a mark. That is why the punctuation has to be load-bearing: without it the two halves would merge back into ordinary lines and the visual argument would be lost. The second option reduces a designed form to a convenience for singers, and the third takes a title for a principle when the device stands on its own. The fourth is the ordinary error of reading a pattern as a failure, which it would be if the line endings varied, and they do not.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader's eye is shown by the marks inside each line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Marvell's To His Coy Mistress and its posthumous printing
questions.learningObjective: infer a poem's intended readership from the collection that first carried it
questions.stem: Andrew Marvell's To His Coy Mistress was first printed in 1681, three years after his death, in a collection of his poems brought out by Robert Boulter, who had also published Milton's Paradise Lost. What does that fact do to the poem's apparent readership?

options.text: It shows the poem was written for a private circle, since a poem printed only after its author's death could never have been meant for the public
options.misconception: infers private intention from posthumous publication, which is a common accident of an archive

options.text: It removes the poem from the history of its own form, since a poem printed three years late belongs to no period's experiments
options.misconception: dates a poem out of its form's history, which is exactly what the printing does not do

options.text: It makes the poem's tone look like a choice rather than a habit, since a collection assembled by an editor selects for a public that was not the poet's own
It shows the poem was written after Marvell's death, since a collection printed in 1681 could only contain recent work
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect, treating the printing date as the writing date

questions.explanation: A poem's tone is easier to read once the audience it was collected for is known. Marvell wrote in the middle decades of the century to people who knew his idiom, and this poem argues in hyperbole, punning on a punning vocabulary, the register of an argument among readers already enjoying it. Publishing that register in 1681, in a collection made by a bookseller, placed it before a public with no such habit of mind, and a public for whom its jokes could read as a plain statement of the case. The book's editor, and the public he served, are therefore part of the poem's reception history even though neither wrote a line of it. Nothing in this makes the poem a different poem: the carpe diem argument it makes is a standard one, and the standard form does not belong to a period alone. The first option draws a private intention from a posthumous printing, which is an accident of custody rather than a fact about the writing. The third and fourth simply misdate the poem and detach it from the tradition it works in.
questions.hint: Ask who met the poem first, and what habits that public had.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The three-movement structure of To His Coy Mistress
questions.learningObjective: restore a syllogistic argument to the order in which it must be heard
questions.stem: Four sections of To His Coy Mistress have been printed out of order. Restore them so that each section answers the one before it, given that the poem is a single argument about time and it moves from what would be possible to what is.

options.text: a section that imagines the lovers spending an absurdly long courtship, allotment by allotment, on the assumption that time is not short

a section that pictures what will be left when both are dead, in which the beauty the suitor has been praising will be beyond finding and the grave is called a good and private room that nobody visits
a section that appeals to what is left now, the skin and the spirit still warm, and asks for the present to be used rather than the future argued about
a section that closes the argument by making its own terms do the work, so that the sun cannot be stopped but can be made to run

questions.explanation: The poem runs as a syllogism, and the order is fixed by the logic rather than by feeling. It opens by granting the largest possible premise: if world and time were unlimited, the suitor would court for a century before the Flood, would spend a hundred years on the eyes, and the coyness would not be a fault at all. That premise is then withdrawn. If the premise holds, the woman has no cause for refusal, and the argument has no purchase. So the second movement supplies the denial, and the denial is built out of the same hyperbole run backwards: a winged chariot is behind him, and ahead lies a desert. The third movement converts the denial into a request, appealing to what is actually present. Only after the appeal does the poem reach the image that closes it, and that image belongs to the end, because it reports a result rather than making a claim. The third option cannot be first because it appeals to the present, which presupposes the contrast; the second cannot be second because it depends on the loss the first has imagined and the third has not yet supplied.
questions.hint: Follow the premise, its denial, the appeal, and then the conclusion.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham and its criticism of the dead man
questions.learningObjective: recognise a critical argument inside a poem of lament
questions.stem: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham, printed in 1684, is twenty-five lines of rhyming couplets on a verse satirist who died at thirty, and it includes the claim that his roughness was a noble error forced on a writer of his strength, and that his early death spared him the finishing that nature never gives the young. What kind of poem is being written?

options.text: A panegyric, since nothing but praise of the dead can properly appear in a poem written to mourn him
options.misconception: restricts elegy to praise, and so cannot see the critical argument inside the poem

options.text: A biographical notice, since the poem's interest lies in the circumstances of a death and the qualities of the dead man
options.misconception: treats a poem's estimate of a writer's quality as mere biography

options.text: A satirical poem, since describing a writer as rough in order to defend him is the ordinary practice of the satirist's trade
options.misconception: infers satire from the vocabulary of roughness, ignoring whom the judgement serves

options.text: A critical poem, since the judgement about an error forced on a writer is a claim about the writing and can be wrong or right

options.text: That the English is a new poem with a borrowed plot, and that the form has been chosen for the new language rather than preserved from the old

options.misconception: assumes a rhyme scheme survives translation, when the form is rebuilt for the new language

options.text: That the originals were written in rhyming verse and the couplets recover what the translators' predecessors had lost
options.misconception: supposes the source was couplets, when the originals are in octosyllabic couplets and rhyme at a different length

options.text: That the collection is an anthology of sources rather than a work, since gathering translations disqualifies the book from being a poem in itself
options.misconception: denies a translated collection the status of a made work, which is exactly what a book of poems is

What the reader receives is a narrative that stands on its own in English, with a shape answerable to English expectations, and an obligation to the original which is to the sequence of events and their relations rather than to the line endings. What does the expansion of 1714 tell a reader?

options.text: That the poem was originally a mistake, since a writer who needs two hundred more lines had got the scale wrong at first
options.misconception: treats a revision as a failure of the first attempt, which is what revision is not

options.text: That the engravings decided the length, since a poem illustrated needs more room than one carried in the head
options.misconception: makes the illustrations the cause of the added cantos

options.text: That the small scale of the incident had been mistaken for the scale of the poem, and that the mock machinery is what puts them right
That the poem is not a mock heroic at all in the 1714 text, since a work with real spirits is a serious supernatural narrative
options.misconception: assumes mock machinery cannot coexist with mock seriousness, which is the definition of the mock heroic

Adding a race of airy and earthly spirits does not enlarge the incident; it enlarges the mismatch, and the mismatch is the poem's subject. The explanatory key published alongside is part of the same construction, since a mock poem that has to explain its own mock gravity is being comic about criticism as well. The 1714 state is therefore a fuller version of the argument rather than a different poem. The fourth assumes the presence of spirits makes a work serious, which is precisely the convention the mock heroic is holding up to ridicule.

questions.topic: Ottava rima distinguished from the Spenserian stanza
questions.learningObjective: tell two nine-line-adjacent stanza forms apart by their rhyme and their last line

stimulus.body: an original ottava rima passage written for this question, printed in the stem
stimulus.license: original text written for this question; no protected text used

questions.stem: A passage written for this question in the stanza Scott used for Rokeby in 1813 runs: "The merchant's brow was scored with care, and he / Would tell of losses he had known at sea: / And every bill he laid before the fire / Told how the harbour of his hope lay bare; / The very mast, said he, I have not seen / Since April, and the harbour-keeper's she / Hangs on the mole, and half the fleet is lost: / This was the sum and substance of his cost." Which statement describes the stanza and distinguishes it from the Spenserian stanza?

options.text: Eight lines of eight syllables rhyming abababcc, with a couplet close; the Spenserian stanza has nine lines all of one length
options.misconception: confuses the syllable count of this form with that of a ballad stanza, and so misstates both forms

options.text: Eight lines of iambic pentameter rhyming abababcc, with a final couplet that closes the octave; the Spenserian stanza has nine lines and a longer last line
Eight lines of iambic pentameter rhyming abababcc, with a couplet that opens a new argument; the Spenserian stanza has nine lines and the same rhyme letters
options.misconception: describes the rhyme letters correctly but then claims the two forms rhyme alike

options.text: Eight lines of iambic pentameter rhyming all in one sound, so that the stanza closes as a single sustained sound; the Spenserian stanza rhymes in pairs
options.misconception: reduces a patterned rhyme scheme to a single sound, which is monorhyme and not ottava rima

questions.explanation: The test that settles it is the ninth line, and the test before that is the rhyme. The passage's ends run care-he, sea-fire, bare-seen, she-lost, cost, which is abababcc: three pairs, then a closing pair. Three pairs give a half-turn and the closing pair gives the full turn, so the couplet is where the stanza's argument is completed rather than started. That is the form Scott used for Rokeby, and it is why the form is congenial to a long narrative: it can end a turn and begin another without a line wasted. The Spenserian stanza is nine lines, the first eight rhyming abab bc and the ninth rhyming with them and running to an extra foot, that is, twelve syllables rather than ten. So the two forms are distinguished twice over, by the number of lines and by what the last line does. The second option gives the right rhyme letters and the wrong syllable count, and then misdescribes the Spenserian stanza as uniform. The third and fourth corrupt the rhyme scheme in ways a reader can disprove on sight.
questions.hint: Count the lines, then count the rhyme pairs, then measure the last line.

questions.learningObjective: read a change in a title page as an editorial decision
questions.stem: Gray's Elegy was published in 1751 with the word Wrote on its title page, and from the eighth edition of 1753 the title page read Written. Nothing in the poem changed. What does the alteration of a single word tell a reader?

options.text: That the poem's date is uncertain, since a word that distinguishes composing from writing implies a distinction about when the poem was made
options.misconception: reads a change of tense as a change of date, when the poem's date is not in question

options.text: That the eighth edition contains a different poem, since a new title page normally accompanies revised text
options.misconception: assumes a new title page means new text, which is a common and expensive error in bibliography

options.text: That the poet asked for the change, since a poet who disliked a word could not have objected until the eighth edition appeared
options.misconception: invents a poet's instruction where the record shows only a printer's decision

options.text: That a later editor judged the title inaccurate, since writing is a general word and the word chosen first claimed more than the poem delivers

questions.explanation: A title page is a publisher's statement about a book, and publishers make these decisions for reasons that are about the book rather than the poem. Wrote is a strong word: it says the poem is the record of an act, that the act happened and the page is its trace. Written is a weaker word, and the change to it reads as a judgement that the first had overclaimed, or at least that the vaguer word would sell without inviting the objection the stronger one invites. Either way the poem is untouched, which is the point: a reader who treats the alteration as evidence of a new text has been misled by the position of the change on the page. The practical lesson for anyone working with printed texts is general. The first option invents a dating problem out of a verb. The fourth attributes a decision to the poet for which there is no evidence at all, and dates it by a book's history rather than by his.
questions.hint: Ask what a publisher is claiming when choosing between the two words.

questions.topic: The couplet every two quatrains in Gray's Elegy

questions.stem: Gray's Elegy is a long lyric in quatrains rhyming abab, and a rhyming couplet follows every second quatrain, so the poem is felt in blocks of ten lines. What does the couplet at the end of each pair of quatrains do?

options.text: It marks a change of speaker, since a couplet between quatrains is the standard English signal that a different voice has taken the poem
options.misconception: treats a stanza unit as a change of voice, which would be a very odd poem indeed

options.text: It resumes the argument, since a couplet of rhymed lines is a place where a poem states a conclusion and the next pair of quatrains takes it up again
It fills out the metre, since ten lines of iambic pentameter need a couplet to complete the count and the poem is written in blocks of that length
options.misconception: explains a structural unit by a numerical convenience, when the count is a result and not a cause

options.text: It separates the poem's topics, since Gray moves from the dead to the living to the reader and the couplet announces each of the three subjects
options.misconception: attributes a content plan to a formal unit, though the poem does not divide that way

questions.explanation: The couplet is the poem's hinge. A quatrain in this form carries a mood or a turn of thought without closing anything, and two of them together accumulate; the couplet then says something short and conclusive, and the next pair of quatrains sets off again. That is why a reader remembers the poem in blocks of ten lines rather than in lines: the couplet is a full stop placed every twenty beats, and the poem's argument is a chain of such stops. The effect on the argument is that the poem keeps returning to a settled position and then unsettling itself, which is a plausible mechanism for a meditation on death and on the ways people console themselves. The second option confuses a formal unit with a change of voice, and the poem's speaker is the same throughout. The third reverses cause and effect, since nobody counts to ten before writing. The fourth finds a content plan that the form does not encode, and a reader who expected three announced subjects would be disappointed.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would miss if the couplets were all removed.

questions.topic: Blake's Songs as a set of hand-coloured copies rather than an edition
questions.learningObjective: reason about what a book means when its copies were made by hand over years
questions.stem: Blake's Songs of Innocence was etched and printed in 1789 and the combined Songs of Innocence and of Experience in 1794, with the verse and the image cut together on the same plate and coloured by Blake and his wife; he went on printing and colouring further copies as patrons ordered them, so the copies differ from one another. What follows for a reader holding one of them?

options.text: That no copy is a copy at all, since a book whose pages differ cannot be a single work with variants
options.misconception: denies that a work can be printed repeatedly with variation, which is the ordinary condition of hand printing

options.text: That the text is secondary to the image, since the plates carry both and the reader who cannot see the image has missed the poem
options.misconception: assumes the image outranks the words because they share a plate

options.text: That the copy in hand is one state among many, and that the differences between copies are evidence about Blake's continuing revisions rather than about the book's intention
That the 1794 title page is a later addition, since a book whose copies differ cannot be dated by the date on its title
options.misconception: infers that a title-page date is unreliable because the copies vary internally

questions.explanation: A book printed from plates that the printer also colours is a different sort of object from a book struck off in editions, and the difference has to be reasoned about rather than assumed away. Because he continued to print and to colour for years, no two copies are identical: some are darker, some have order written in at the corner, some were left in outline for a patron to finish. Those differences are evidence about a process that ran on for decades, and a careful editor uses one copy against another to establish what was altered and when. What a reader cannot do is treat a difference as a mistake to be corrected, or read the title-page date as meaningless. The second option refuses the possibility of variation, the third makes the image a substitute for the verse, and the last confuses a stable imprint with a stable impression, two things bibliographers keep carefully apart.
questions.hint: Ask what a second copy of the same book can tell you that one cannot.

questions.topic: The 1800 second state of Lyrical Ballads and its added prefaces
questions.learningObjective: read a second edition as a change of theory rather than of contents
questions.stem: Lyrical Ballads appeared in 1798 with a short preface, and the expanded edition of 1800 replaced it with a longer preface plus further essays setting out the writers' account of what poetry is and how it is composed. What does the enlargement tell a reader about the first edition?

options.text: That the authors had begun by implying a theory and had by 1800 chosen to state it, so the poems can be read against an account they did not have to publish
That the 1798 preface was an afterthought, since a theory this long could only have been written once the poems were on sale
options.misconception: dates a preface by its length, when a short preface can precede a book by years

options.text: That the 1800 essays withdraw the poems from the market, since a stated theory turns a collection of songs into a treatise
options.misconception: supposes that stating a theory withdraws the poems from readers, which is the opposite of the effect

options.text: That a reviewer objected to the 1798 preface, since publishers lengthen prefaces only under pressure from critics
options.misconception: invents a reviewing dispute where the record shows a deliberate change of plan

questions.hint: Ask what the 1800 essays let a reader do that the 1798 preface forbade.

options.misconception: reads a theory of composition as a guarantee of access to a private state

options.text: To prefer short words, since ordinary speech is made of short words and the test is therefore a test of vocabulary length
options.misconception: reduces a claim about idiom to a claim about word length

options.text: To accept the poem on the poet's word, since a stated theory binds the critic to take the author's account of the writing as true
options.misconception: makes a critical position into a duty to believe the writer

options.text: To find out whether a poem's words would pass for speech, since the test is a linguistic one and a critic can apply it without knowing the author's circumstances

questions.learningObjective: judge a writer's account of his own process as evidence with a shape
questions.stem: In his literary autobiography, Wordsworth tells a poet friend that when he came to the spot in the Lakes where a friend had died, the two lines that close that friend's story came into his head before he had formed any intention of writing, and that afterwards he composed the rest to serve them. What is the shape of that claim?

options.text: It is a claim about the writer's memory, and it stands or falls with the reliability of his recollection of a walk taken with a friend
options.misconception: treats a claim about the order of composition as a claim about the reliability of a recollection

options.text: It is a claim that a specific pair of lines has priority over everything else in the poem, and a critic can test it by asking whether the rest of the poem serves those lines or is served by them
It is an apology for a poem that other people disliked, since an account of accident is a way of disowning responsibility for the result
options.misconception: reads a claim about process as a rhetorical move to escape responsibility

options.text: It is a piece of evidence that the Lake poems are translations of something older, since lines that arrive already made cannot be composed

questions.hint: Ask what follows for the poem's earlier stanzas if two lines are its origin.

questions.learningObjective: read a writer's account of his own process as a rhetorical construction

What does the preface do for the poem?

options.misconception: uses the preface to answer a complaint about length, which is not the purpose the preface serves

options.text: It supplies a source for the poem's images, so that a reader who wants to trace them to the travel book can do so and find the poem explained
options.misconception: treats the preface as a source note, when it describes a mental process rather than a text

options.text: It makes the poem's incompleteness part of what the poem is about, since a text that announces its own loss has claimed the loss as its subject

The preface is not an apology and not a source note; it is a second short poem, or at any rate a text whose argument is that what is missing is part of what is present. The second option is the ordinary reading and it misses the mechanism, since nobody needs persuading about length once the loss has been given a shape. The fourth mistakes explanation for accessibility, which is precisely what a dream resists.
questions.hint: Ask what the preface asks the reader to measure the surviving text against.

options.text: It shows that the poem was written to be sung, since a minstrel who sings cannot have intended his audience to read silently

options.text: An archive, since a manuscript collection is by definition an archive and an archive makes no claims about what it holds
options.misconception: confuses a printed collection with a repository, and removes the prefaces by definition

questions.explanation: A collection of ballads with prose prefaces is not a neutral store. The prefaces state where each song came from, which versions exist, and why the editor prefers one, and that is a series of claims about evidence which a reader can accept, reject or narrow. Some of the claims are about age, and there the honest position is that the editor is arguing a case, because a song's age is rarely established by the manuscript that carries it. The songs themselves are the other half of the argument, since a reader who has heard the tunes can judge the claim independently of the prose. That is what makes the collection historically important: it made a body of oral material available in print and, in doing so, had to argue for it. The first option believes that transcription is a neutral act, which is the belief the prefaces exist to argue against. The third leaps from arrangement to invention, which is a serious charge to bring and is not established. The fourth treats a printed book as a repository and so dismisses the very evidence the book is made of.
questions.hint: Ask what a preface that argues for a song's age is doing to a reader's trust.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and the change of speaker in its later cantos
questions.learningObjective: track a change of voice across a poem's successive books
questions.stem: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage appeared in 1812 in two cantos, and the poet added a third and then a fourth canto years later, revising the whole poem; in the later additions the surveying traveller of the first two cantos is largely replaced by a figure who has begun to look at his own country as a stranger might. What does that change do?

options.text: It makes the poem a satire on the places it visits, since a traveller who criticises what he sees has stopped being a traveller
options.misconception: confuses the poem's judgements about places with judgements on a speaker, which are different objects

options.text: It spoils the poem, since a poem whose speaker changes is a poem in which no voice can be trusted throughout
options.misconception: treats a developed speaker as an unreliable one, which are separate charges

options.text: It makes the poem self-applying, since the person describing the world's sadness is now visibly part of the world being described
It leaves the poem unchanged, since the later cantos are additions and a reader of the first two will never see them
options.misconception: ignores the revision of the earlier cantos, which is what the change consisted in

questions.explanation: The move worth naming is the poem turning its own instrument on itself. In the early cantos a young man surveys ruins and complains about the present, which puts him outside the world he is measuring. When the same figure begins to include himself among the things that time has used up, the surveying is no longer neutral, and every complaint about a ruined empire acquires a second application, since the speaker is inside the ruin he is describing. That is a large structural change and it is why the additions had to be accompanied by a revision of what came before: the earlier cantos could not stay in the old voice once the new one existed. The first option mistakes a judgement about a place for a judgement about a person. The third treats a change of voice as a collapse of voice, which would condemn most long poems. The fourth misses the revision, which is the point of the item.
questions.hint: Ask where the speaker now stands in relation to what he is describing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Don Juan printed in a periodical and left unfinished
questions.learningObjective: read a serialised, unfinished work's form as a consequence of its printing
questions.stem: Byron's Don Juan began appearing in a periodical in 1819 and was never finished; sixteen cantos were published in his lifetime and a further five after his death, and the poem's line numbering is arranged so that a reader can see where it breaks off. What does the form owe to the conditions of its printing?

options.text: Nothing, since a poem's shape is settled before it is printed and the periodical merely delivered a finished work more slowly
options.misconception: insists that a poem's form is independent of its mode of publication, which the interrupted line numbering denies

options.text: The subject, since a work published in parts must be about a subject that can be broken off and resumed without damage
options.misconception: infers subject matter from a printing arrangement, which is not how subject works

options.text: The authorship, since an unfinished work in a periodical was evidently a collaboration whose parts nobody owned
options.misconception: turns a publishing arrangement into a claim about who wrote the poem

options.text: The irregularity of the verse, since a poem delivered in instalments and never concluded cannot pretend to the completeness an instalment-by-instalment arrival usually implies

questions.explanation: The formal point of Don Juan is that it behaves like a conversation and is printed like one. A serial in a periodical arrives in instalments at intervals, is read in instalments, and can be abandoned between them; a poem built on digression and on a speaker who keeps introducing himself can exploit that, since each instalment can be a fresh turn rather than a chapter. The visible break in the numbering is the honest signal at the end, and it is the same fact the readers of the period had: the work is not going to finish, and the text says so instead of pretending. That is not a failure of composition but a composition, and it is why the poem's metre and its delivery are so well matched. The first option claims independence from printing, which is exactly what the interrupted numbering refutes. The third and fourth both convert a fact about publication into a fact about content or authorship, which is the commonest way this material is misread.
questions.hint: Ask what the interrupted numbering tells a reader at the end of the text.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ozymandias and the rhyme the octave never resolves
questions.learningObjective: read an unresolved rhyme as a structural fact about a sonnet
questions.stem: Shelley's Ozymandias, printed in The Examiner on 11 January 1818, is a fourteen-line sonnet whose rhyme scheme is ABABACDCEDEFEF: the C rhyme occurs on lines five and seven, is answered nowhere, and the couplet at the end is EF. What has the form done to the poem?

options.text: Broken the sonnet, since a rhyme scheme that is not the expected one is by definition not a sonnet any more
options.misconception: supposes a sonnet is defined by its rhyme scheme rather than by its length and metre

options.text: Left a rhyme hanging in the octave, so that the reader carries an unfinished sound out of the first half and into a second half that never resolves it
Hidden the poem's argument, since a scheme that varies from the usual conceals the sense as well as the sound
options.misconception: believes a rhyme scheme can prevent comprehension of the sentences

options.text: Signalled that the poem is unfinished, since a rhyme left unanswered is a sign that the writer stopped early
options.misconception: reads an unresolved rhyme as evidence of incompletion, when the poem ends with a full couplet

questions.explanation: An unresolved rhyme is a sound with nowhere to go, and a reader of verse hears that. Here the C rhyme is placed exactly where an ordinary sonnet would be turning towards its couplet, and it is not answered, so the octave closes on an open sound. The poem's content and its form are doing the same thing: what survives is a fragment, and the two legs of the statue are described as standing without the body they belonged to, so the shape of the verse enacts the shape of the ruin. The final couplet then does real work, supplying the closure the octave withheld, which is why EF at the end is not the poem's final word but its resolution. The second option defines a sonnet by rhyme rather than by line count and metre, which would make a great many sonnets into something else. The third confuses pattern with sense, since the sentences are perfectly plain. The fourth mistakes a structural opening for an unfinished job.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader does with a rhyme that is never answered.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The chained rhyme of the five sections of the Ode to the West Wind
questions.learningObjective: explain what an interlocking rhyme across sections buys a long lyric
questions.stem: The Ode to the West Wind is written as five sections, and in each section the four tercets are linked so that the middle line of one tercet rhymes with the outer lines of the next, ABA BCB CDC DED, followed by a rhyming couplet. What does the linking do across the length of the poem?

options.text: It saves syllables, since a rhyme already available in the preceding tercet costs a writer less than a new one
options.misconception: explains a structural choice by an economy of composition, which the pattern does not require

options.text: It makes the sections parts of one movement, since each new tercet is obliged to pick up a sound already sounding and cannot start over in a fresh key
It marks the sections as separate, since a rhyme that runs across the break tells the reader where one section ends and the next begins
options.misconception: describes the linking as marking boundaries, when it does the opposite

options.text: It makes the poem a fixed form, since a rhyme pattern that governs every section turns free verse into a verse form with rules
options.misconception: converts a rhyme pattern into a rule-bound stanza form, which is not what an interlocking rhyme is

questions.explanation: The point of the chained rhyme is that a single sound is carried forward across the whole poem, so nothing in the fourth section can be begun in a register unrelated to what the first section established. That is a considerable constraint on a poem whose subject is a wind, a subject that invites loose motion and shifting tone, and it converts that invitation into a form that keeps turning back on itself. The closing couplet of each section is what makes the pattern possible, because it gathers the thread before the next section takes it up, and the poem's last couplet therefore does a formal as well as a rhetorical job. The second option gives a mechanical reason for a formal choice, which is the wrong level. The third reverses the effect, since a rhyme crossing a break joins rather than divides. The fourth confuses a pattern with a form: a fixed form has a stanza shape and a line count, and this poem has neither.
questions.hint: Ask what a new tercet is obliged to do because of the tercet before it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prometheus Unbound and the kind of work its subtitle announces
questions.learningObjective: read a subtitle as a promise about a work's kind
questions.stem: Shelley's Prometheus Unbound, printed in 1820, is subtitled A Lyrical Drama in Four Acts, and its hero is freed from the penalty of a Greek play and becomes a voice arguing with the ruler of the world about the possibility of improvement. What does the subtitle promise that a reader can hold the book to?

options.text: That the work will be verse organised into acts, so a reader can check the division of the argument against the division of the text and see whether the four acts make a shape
That the work is a play and can be judged by how it would work on a stage, since the word drama settles the question of what kind of thing has been written
options.misconception: treats the word drama as a promise of performance, ignoring that the poem's verse resists the stage

options.text: That the work is a translation of an older play, since a subtitle naming a Greek figure is a signal that a source is being reworked
options.misconception: infers translation from the presence of a Greek figure in a subtitle

options.text: That the work is one of a series, since a numbered act in a subtitle implies other works with other numbers attached to the same project
options.misconception: reads a number in a subtitle as evidence of a series

questions.explanation: A subtitle is a promise a reader can check, and this one is checkable in a way that matters. Lyrical means the work will be built out of lyric intensities rather than plot; drama means it will be divided into acts and will move through argument; in four acts fixes the shape and says in advance how many joints it has. That last is the useful part, because a four-act verse argument can be tested: are the four sections of comparable weight, do they turn rather than simply continue, and does the last act deliver what the first promised. A reader who finds the acts uneven has found something, and has found it using the work's own stated measure rather than an imported one. The first option treats the word as a performance guarantee, which the verse form itself resists. The third and fourth invent obligations from the Greek name and from a number, neither of which carries a promise of that kind.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can count in the text and check against the subtitle.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The five ten-line stanzas of the Ode on a Grecian Urn
questions.learningObjective: read a stanza's length and its half-line as a claim about indeterminacy
questions.stem: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, printed in 1819, is five stanzas of ten lines, and in each stanza the fourth and fifth lines are a pair of which the fifth stands alone, set off, and is related to the fourth by a near-rhyme rather than a full one. What has the stanza made of the questions it keeps asking?

options.text: A closed structure, since five stanzas of ten lines is a shape the reader can predict and predictability is what an argument about uncertainty needs
options.misconception: assumes a regular shape settles a poem whose subject is unsettled

options.text: A counted structure, since the poem's ten lines per stanza can be used to check whether the poet kept the same number in every case
options.misconception: reduces a formal device to a matter of counting, which is a check and not a reading

options.text: A structure that argues the poem's subject, since a question followed by a near answer and then by another question models a mind that cannot settle
An unfinished structure, since a near-rhyme standing in for a full rhyme is a sign the poet could not find the rhyme he wanted
options.misconception: reads a designed near-rhyme as a failure to find a rhyme

questions.explanation: The stanza is built to prevent closure, and the two devices work together. The fifth line is lifted out of the run and left standing, so the rhythm itself hesitates at the exact point where an answer would arrive; and it is tied to the fourth by a sound that almost matches without matching, so the ear is given a promise the poem does not keep. A poem about figures on a vessel who never arrive, never leave, never age and never die is therefore given a form that will not arrive at rest. That is the sense in which the form argues the subject rather than merely housing it, and it is why a reader who counts the stanzas learns nothing beyond a fact about typography. The second option claims a regular shape produces a settled effect. The third mistakes a check for an interpretation. The fourth reads a designed effect as an unmet intention, which is the standard error about near-rhyme.
questions.hint: Ask what the set-off fifth line does to the rhythm at the point of answer.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Bright Star printed seventeen years after Keats's death
questions.learningObjective: read a late first publication as evidence about a poem's reception
questions.stem: Keats's sonnet Bright Star was first published in a Plymouth newspaper in 1838, seventeen years after its author died, while a friend maintained for decades that it was the last poem he wrote. What does the gap between composition and first publication make difficult?

options.text: Fixing the date of the poem, since a first printed date of 1838 cannot be reconciled with any claim about the author's last months
options.misconception: supposes a printing date settles a composition date, when it does not

options.text: Deciding who wrote it, since a poem published long after an author's death can easily be attributed to the wrong member of a circle
options.misconception: raises a misattribution problem the record does not present

options.text: Judging the manuscript copies, since a handwritten text is by definition less reliable than a printed one
options.misconception: ranks manuscript below print without argument, which is a habit rather than a principle

options.text: Establishing which of the manuscript versions is the finished one, since a poem circulating in manuscript for seventeen years can be revised at any point in that time

questions.explanation: A poem that reaches print seventeen years after it was written has had a long life in manuscript, and manuscript is a form that carries its own revisions. Different hands copy it, different friends are asked to keep it, and a poet who has stopped revising still has readers who press for copies; the result is a poem with more than one state and no printed text to arbitrate between them. That is the practical difficulty, and it is why the competing claims about which version is final can be so persistent. The friend's belief about the poem being the last written is a different kind of claim altogether, resting on a particular copy and on recollection, and it is not refuted by the printing date; the two questions are about text and about date, and confusing them produces a great deal of unproductive argument. The second option assumes publication dates settle composition dates. The third and fourth propose problems the evidence does not raise.
questions.hint: Ask what a poem does to its text during seventeen years in manuscript.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: La Belle Dame sans Merci in a weekly periodical, with a headnote
questions.learningObjective: read a periodical printing as an editorial framing the poet did not write
questions.stem: Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci was first printed in May 1820 in a weekly periodical edited by a poet who was also the poet's friend, with a long introductory note about courtly love and an age he contrasts with the present, and the poem appeared anonymously. What does that printing do to the poem?

options.text: It removes the poem from history, since a poem printed in a weekly magazine is journalism and journalism is not literature
options.misconception: denies a periodical printing any literary standing, which the poem's reception in that very form disproves

options.text: It gives the poem a frame the poet did not write, so that the first thing a reader met was a critical position and the poem had to be read inside someone else's argument
It makes the poem anonymous in fact, since an unsigned poem in a magazine has no author and can be reprinted by anyone
options.misconception: confuses unsigned with authorless, which are quite different states

options.text: It proves the poem was written for the periodical, since a poem that appears in a weekly is a poem composed for a weekly's readers
options.misconception: infers the occasion of composition from the place of first publication

questions.explanation: A poem printed beside an essay is read in the essay's company, and here the essay does real work: it places the poem among older poems about a lady who will not be won and then contrasts that older world with the present, which is a reading of the poem supplied before the poem begins. That is a gift to a reader who has no context and a frame on a reader who has opinions, and it is not the poet's frame. The signature used was a joke rather than an attempt at concealment, which matters, because it separates the question of who wrote the poem from the question of who wrote the note. The note is also evidence about how the poem was received in its own year, which is a kind of history no later edition can supply. The second option dismisses a whole mode of publication. The third and fourth each confuse a printing circumstance with a fact about the writing.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader meets first, and who wrote it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The stanza of In Memoriam as a long quatrain followed by a short one
questions.learningObjective: read an alternation of long and short lines as a claim about weight
questions.stem: In Memoriam, published in 1850, is built from stanzas of eight lines in which four lines of four beats are followed by four lines of three beats, rhyming abba and then bcbc, and the poem runs to more than a hundred such stanzas. What does the repeated alternation do to a poem of that length?

options.text: It makes the poem monotonous, since a stanza repeated more than a hundred times can only be a failure of invention
options.misconception: judges a form by the number of its repetitions, which is the argument against every fixed form

options.text: It fragments the poem, since a change of line length inside a stanza cannot help but break the argument in two
options.misconception: treats a change of line length as a break in the argument rather than a shape for it

options.text: It gives the poem a weight that can be carried, since the first quatrain can state something at length and the second can close it, over and over, without exhausting the reader
It records the date, since a poem written over seventeen years needs a form that can show how much of it belongs to which year
options.misconception: supposes the form encodes a chronology, which nothing in the stanza indicates

questions.explanation: The alternation gives the poem a unit that is large enough to hold a thought and small enough to be repeated indefinitely. Four beats can state a case, three beats can register the recoil from it, and the two rhyme pairs close each quatrain without closing the stanza, so a reader is given a completion and a continuation at once, several thousand times over. That is the practical answer to the length of the book: a form that can be used a hundred times without being noticed as a repetition, because what is repeated is a rhythm of weight rather than a pattern of images. The poem's subject, a dead friend and the years after the death, is well served by a stanza that can hold an argument and then let it down a step. The second option makes monotony a sufficient objection to a fixed form, which would rule out most English verse. The third and fourth misattribute to the form a fragmentation and a chronology it does not encode.
questions.hint: Ask what the second quatrain does that the first one has just finished with.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The title of In Memoriam and the year it carries
questions.learningObjective: read a title's Roman numeral as a documented piece of information
questions.stem: Tennyson's book was published in 1850 under a title that names its subject by initials and carries a Roman numeral for a year, and the poems inside had been written and rewritten over the seventeen years before publication. What does the title give a reader that the poems themselves do not?

options.text: The name of the dead man, given in full in the title so that no reader need look it up in a preface
options.misconception: misreads initials as a spelled-out name, which is the opposite of what initials are for

options.text: The order of the poems, since a title naming a year must also fix the sequence of the stanzas beneath it
options.misconception: supposes a title that gives a year also gives an order

options.text: The poem's metre, since a title naming a year is a date and a date fixes the form that was current
options.misconception: infers a form from a date, which says nothing about the stanza a poet chose

options.text: The date of the death, given as a numeral in the title and therefore not a matter of a reader's inference from the poems

questions.explanation: The title does a small and precise job: it dates the loss rather than the book. A Roman numeral in a title is a piece of information that a reader does not have to reconstruct, and reconstructing it is exactly the kind of work a title exists to save. The fact that the poems were written and rewritten across seventeen years before publication is what makes the distinction worth making, because the year on the title and the year on the imprint are twenty years apart, and a reader who has learned to read dates off title pages will conflate them. Nothing in the sequence of stanzas carries the date, and nothing in the title carries the sequence, which is why the two halves of the title are doing separate jobs. The second option reads initials as a name, which is the opposite of their function. The third and fourth both extract information from a date that the title does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask which year the title dates, and which year the title page does not.
