questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Lady of Shalott and its two printed states
questions.learningObjective: read two states of one poem as an argument about which is the poem
questions.stem: Tennyson's The Lady of Shalott was first printed in 1833 and reprinted revised in the two-volume Poems of 1842, and the 1842 text is the one usually read; each state is a five-line stanza in which four lines run to eight syllables and a fifth runs to six. What does the existence of the two states oblige a reader to do?

options.text: Prefer the later text, since a revised text is by definition the poet's final intention and the earlier one is a draft
options.misconception: assumes a revision records a final intention, which is a claim no text can prove

options.text: Choose a text and say which, since a reader who quotes without naming the state has made a claim about a poem that the poem's history does not support
Read both together, since two states of one poem are one poem and a reader who reads only one has read half of it
options.misconception: makes a practical necessity into an aesthetic doctrine

options.text: Ignore the earlier text, since an 1842 printing is by that date the standard and a standard needs no history
options.misconception: treats a fact about a copy in a library as a fact about the poem

questions.explanation: Two states is a normal condition for a revised poem and it puts one obligation on a reader, which is to declare which one is being discussed. Nothing else follows from it. The later text is not thereby the poet's settled intention, because a revision can correct a detail and break a passage elsewhere, and the earlier text is not thereby a draft, because a printed text is a finished thing that other people read and wrote about. What the pair does give a reader is history: the differences between the two states are evidence about what the poet thought was wrong, and that evidence is often more interesting than either state alone. The stanza itself is unchanged in principle, four eight-syllable lines and a six-syllable line, which is a shape that suits a poem about a woman looking out of a tower at a river that carries her away: a long line to hold the looking, a short one to mark the end of the stanza's reach. The second and fourth options treat recency as authority. The third makes an argument out of an inconvenience.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must be able to say for a quotation to be checkable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Ring and the Book told by the people in it
questions.learningObjective: read a narrative given by its participants as a claim about objectivity
questions.stem: Browning's The Ring and the Book, published in four volumes between 1868 and 1869, is made of twelve books, ten of which are spoken by people involved in the events, each giving his own account, and the first and last books are the poet's. What does that arrangement do to the question of what really happened?

options.text: It turns it into a matter of judgement, since agreement is not available and a reader must weigh incompatible accounts on their internal evidence
It makes the question unanswerable and says so, since no two of the accounts agree and a reader is left to choose between witnesses rather than to learn what occurred
options.misconception: concludes that competing accounts leave nothing, when what they leave is a judgement

options.text: It settles it, since the poet's own books at the beginning and end can arbitrate between the participants' versions
options.misconception: supposes the framing narrator is a referee, when the framing is a story about how the story was found

options.text: It avoids it, since a poem that gives every side a voice is declaring that the question does not matter and that all versions are equally true
options.misconception: mistakes a refusal to adjudicate for a claim that all accounts are equally good

questions.explanation: The arrangement is not a failure to reach a fact. It is a decision about how a fact about character is to be established, and the decision is that the only witnesses are interested ones. Each speaker has a stake, a vocabulary and a way of seeing, and the poem's method is to let the stake show by letting the speaker talk for as long as his particular case requires. What a reader gets is not a record but a set of records, and the work done on them is comparison: where two accounts agree, something is probably so; where they diverge, the divergence is usually about what a person was thinking rather than about what happened, and that is the more interesting finding. The poet's own books at the beginning and the end establish where the volume came from and what a reader is being asked to do, and they are not a referee, since the man who found the book is also the man who is reporting what it cost him. The first and fourth options both overstate the result. The third mistakes a frame for an arbiter.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to do when the witnesses disagree.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Hopkins's stress metrics and the regularity beneath the irregularity
questions.learningObjective: tell a difference that looks irregular from one that is not
questions.stem: Hopkins's The Windhover was written in 1877 and not printed until 1918, in a form that asks each line to carry four stresses while the number of syllables in a line varies. What is the reader being trained to hear?

options.text: A line whose length is fixed, since four stresses in every line means four feet in every line and a foot is two syllables
options.misconception: converts a stress count into a syllable count, which is the assumption the form refuses

options.text: A poem that has abandoned metre, since a line whose syllables vary cannot be brought under any rule at all
options.misconception: supposes that variable length abolishes pattern, when the pattern is in the stresses

options.text: A regularity that lives in the count of stresses rather than the count of syllables, so the ear learns to march by the beat and not by the bar
A dialect, since Hopkins insisted that the poem should be read in his own county's accent and the accent is what sets the stresses
options.misconception: turns a claim about accent into a claim about line length, which are different matters

questions.explanation: The useful description of this form is that the rule and the surface disagree on purpose. Four stresses to a line is a rule, and a strict one; the number of syllables is not fixed and is not meant to be. So a reader who counts syllables hears irregularity and a reader who counts beats hears a march, and the poem depends on the second reader. That also explains why such a form was not printed for thirty years: it asks an audience to give up a counting habit it had been taught by English verse since Chaucer, and to learn a different one before the poem can be enjoyed. The second option is the standard confusion, since a foot is not a fixed number of syllables in a language where the stresses are on the vowels. The third mistakes surface irregularity for the absence of a system. The fourth turns a claim about pronunciation into a claim about length, which is the argument the poem's syntax makes impossible.
questions.hint: Ask which count stays constant and which count is allowed to move.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Swinburne's unrhymed five-foot tercets
questions.learningObjective: recognise what a form drops and what it makes necessary in compensation
questions.stem: Swinburne's Ave at que Vale, printed in 1867, is a long lament in tercets of unrhymed five-foot lines, so that consecutive tercets are held together by the movement of the syntax rather than by a returning sound. What follows for a reader?

options.text: The poem cannot be read aloud, since unrhymed verse has no audible pattern and a poem heard without a pattern is not heard at all
options.misconception: supposes unrhymed verse is inaudible, which is a claim about nothing

options.text: The tercet loses its identity, since a unit defined only by the absence of a feature is not a unit at all
options.misconception: denies that a negative definition can be a real formal definition

options.text: The poem is a translation, since unrhymed verse in English is the mark of a poem carried over from a language that rhymes differently
options.misconception: infers translation from the absence of rhyme

options.text: The line-ending carries less of the burden of marking time, so the reader's sense of where one unit stops and the next begins comes from the sense and the pause

questions.explanation: Rhyme in English verse is a clock, and removing it does not remove time; it moves the marking elsewhere. The ears lose the recurring sound that told a reader a unit was closing, and the hands take over: a line now ends where the syntax ends, and a tercet is perceived as a unit because a thought completes in it and the next begins. That is a real demand on a reader, and it is why this kind of writing rewards a reader who will read a line at a time. It is also why the form suits a lament: the continuous syntactic movement holds together a sequence of tercets that rhyme would otherwise have welded. Nothing about the form is inaudible; a poem read aloud without rhyme is still a poem heard, with the pauses doing the work. The second option is an absurdity dressed as a difficulty. The third denies that a form can be defined negatively, which is how most modern verse is defined. The fourth reads a formal absence as evidence of a foreign source.
questions.hint: Ask what marks the end of a unit once the rhyme has gone.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The date of Hardy's Darkling Thrush as an evidence problem
questions.learningObjective: weigh a manuscript against a printing when they disagree
questions.stem: Hardy's The Darkling Thrush was printed on 29 December 1900, while the manuscript carries a year that has been struck out, which if it stood would date the poem to the previous year. What is the state of the evidence, and what does it support?

options.text: The two dates are equally secure, so a reader must choose between them and there is no principled way to prefer either
options.misconception: makes the two kinds of evidence equally strong, when one is a dated printing and one is a corrected manuscript

options.text: The printing date is secure and the poem is a work of 1900; the manuscript may be corrected, and a later print record is evidence a reader can check
Neither date can be used, since a poem whose manuscript is corrected must have been written more than once and the first writing is unknowable
options.misconception: infers that a corrected manuscript destroys the date rather than supporting one

options.text: The manuscript date is the better evidence, since a writer knows when he wrote a poem and a printer knows only when he printed it
options.misconception: prefers the writer's recollection to a dated printing as a general rule, which is not a rule

questions.explanation: A dated printing is a fact about a book that anyone can look up; a manuscript with a struck-out date is a fact about a moment of revision, and the striking-out is itself the significant thing, since somebody decided the year was not right. That makes the printing the better anchor, and it is the kind of anchor a reader should prefer, because it does not depend on interpretation. It does not follow that the poem cannot have begun the previous year; a writer revising the date on a manuscript is not erasing a composition, and a reader who wants the finer chronology can note the possibility without pretending the two kinds of evidence weigh the same. The second option is the symmetrical error, treating a struck-out manuscript date as equal to a dated printing. The third turns revision into a loss of information. The fourth states a plausible-sounding principle that no one applies as a rule, since writers misdate as often as printers misprint.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two records can be checked by looking it up.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Frost's repeated line and the three-beat lines around it
questions.learningObjective: read a formal repetition as an argument rather than a decoration
questions.stem: Frost's Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, printed in 1923, is four four-line stanzas in which the lines run on three and four beats alternately, and the last line of the first stanza is repeated as the last line of the last. What does the repetition do?

options.text: It saves the poet from writing a fourth stanza, since a repeated line can stand in for the missing one at no cost to the reader
options.misconception: reduces a formal decision to a saving in effort

options.text: It confuses the order of the stanzas, since a reader who meets the same words twice will not know whether the poem has gone backwards
options.misconception: supposes a repetition damages sequence, which it does not

options.text: It makes the poem's two hours and the reader's own position the same thing, since the line that opens the poem's account comes back as the poem's last word
It marks a rhyme, since two lines that end with the same words are a rhyme in the plainest sense of the word
options.misconception: confuses repetition of a whole line with rhyming of line endings, which are different things

questions.explanation: The repeated line is where the poem's two subjects meet. The stanzas describe a man standing in the woods being tempted to stop, and the last line of the first stanza states the distance he has to travel; the last line of the last states the depth of the snow between him and the house. Printing one at the beginning and the other at the end is not economy, since the repetition is what makes the two comparable: the same words carry the journey out and the journey back, and a reader who has the poem in the ear hears a single line doing two jobs at once. The varying beats of the lines, three and four in alternation, keep the poem from settling into a lilt at the moment the temptation is at its strongest, so form and subject are at cross purposes in a way the reader can feel. The second option reduces a structural decision to economy, the third mistakes recurrence for disorder, and the fourth confuses a repeated line with a rhyme.
questions.hint: Ask what the two occurrences of the line are each measuring.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Bishop's One Art and the refrain the villanelle is built to change
questions.learningObjective: read an alteration in a fixed form as the form's own argument
questions.stem: Bishop's One Art, printed in 1976, keeps the architecture of the villanelle, in which two refrains recur until they gather in a closing couplet, but the refrains are altered at nearly every recurrence and the poem's rhyme changes sound in the last tercets. What is the form being used for?

options.text: To be displayed, since a reader who can name the form has shown that the poet could work inside a rule while escaping its strictest requirement
options.misconception: makes the poem a display of technical accomplishment rather than an argument

options.text: To be abandoned halfway, since a poem that keeps the shape but not the rules has failed to keep the form and might as well not have used it
options.misconception: supplies a rule about forms that no one enforces, including their authors

options.text: To be outgrown, since a poet writing in 1976 has options a poet writing a villanelle in the seventeenth century did not, and using the old form shows a debt
options.misconception: assumes later poets are free of forms their predecessors used

options.text: To be argued with, since a form that obliges a phrase to come back unchanged, and then watches it come back changed, is a form that has something to say about loss and habit

questions.explanation: A villanelle's contract is unusually strict: two refrains that must return and must finally join. Keeping the architecture while altering the words at each return puts the poem in a position where a reader can feel the contract and watch it being renegotiated, and the poem's subject, a speaker trying to hold a losing thing steady by repeating a formula, is exactly what that position describes. That is why the rhyme shifting near the end matters: the sound the poem has been leaning on withdraws at the point where the speaker most needs it. The reader therefore gets an argument out of a form rather than a display of skill in one, and the difference matters because the argument is available to anyone who has met the form and does not require a special vocabulary. The second option reduces that to technical display, which would make the alteration decorative. The third invents a rule that forms do not have. The fourth assumes later writers escape earlier forms, which is the opposite of what the form's survival shows.
questions.hint: Ask what a strict form lets a poem say about things that will not stay still.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The two unequal stanzas of Stevens's Snow Man
questions.learningObjective: read a stanza's proportions as part of a poem's argument
questions.stem: Stevens's The Snow Man, written in 1921 and printed in 1923, consists of an eight-line stanza and a three-line stanza, with no rhyme in either and the same subject treated in each. What does the second stanza do that an equal one could not?

options.text: It repairs the first, since a poem that begins too long is corrected by a coda of the right size
options.misconception: treats a stanza as an error and a coda as a patch

options.text: It ends the poem by doing less, since a three-line stanza can carry a single judgement and an eight-line stanza can only keep adding qualifications
It marks the poem's subject twice, since a reader who has met the same man in both stanzas has been given a repetition and a repetition is a technique
options.misconception: names a repetition and treats it as the whole effect, missing the change in scale

options.text: It introduces rhyme, since a short stanza is the standard place for a poem to find its rhyming and it usually supplies one here
options.misconception: supplies a rhyme the poem does not have, since neither stanza rhymes

questions.explanation: The proportions are the argument. The long stanza accumulates: it adds clause to clause, qualification to qualification, and the accumulation is itself a picture of a mind that cannot stop adding. The short stanza can only do one thing, and so it does one thing, which is to state the consequence without another clause. A reader who had met the same judgement set out in eight lines would have been given the material to absorb; a reader who meets it in three has been given the result. That is the whole craft of the poem's shape, and it is why the poem is remembered for its proportions as much as for its content. The second option makes the form a repair job, which misunderstands that the two stanzas are two operations, not one operation and a patch. The third stops at noticing a repetition and misses the change in scale. The fourth adds a rhyme the poem does not contain, which is exactly what a reader who has only read summaries does.
questions.hint: Ask what a stanza of three lines can do that a stanza of eight cannot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Waste Land's two first printings in 1922 and 1923
questions.learningObjective: read a magazine printing and a book printing as different events
questions.stem: Eliot's The Waste Land appeared in an October 1922 issue of a quarterly review and in a November 1922 issue of an American magazine, and its first appearance as a book was in September 1923 from a small private press in an edition of about four hundred and sixty copies. What does that sequence tell a reader about the poem's first audience?

options.text: That the magazine printings were abridgements, since a poem that needed a book to be complete cannot have been complete in a magazine
options.misconception: assumes a magazine printing must be shortened, which is not what a magazine printing is

options.text: That the book printing is the real first edition, since only a book can be called an edition of a poem
options.misconception: defines edition in a way that would leave periodical printing outside literary history

options.text: That it was first read by people who already agreed, since a quarterly review and a literary magazine both reach a readership that has chosen its own kind of reading
That the private press was chosen to make money, since a small edition at a high price is a normal commercial decision
options.misconception: assigns a commercial motive to a private press without evidence, and misses what a small edition is for

questions.explanation: The first audience is the audience of the periodicals, and that fact constrains what a reader can claim about the poem's effect. A quarterly review and a literary magazine reach people who read criticism, who are used to allusion, and who will have met the scholarly book the poem's notes lean on. A poem addressed to that readership can be as difficult as this one is, because difficulty is not the same as exclusion. The small private book printing that came a year later was not the commercial event and was never intended to be: about four hundred and sixty copies, from a press run by friends, is a book designed to be complete and to be owned, and it is a very different object from the instalment a reader met in a magazine. The second option invents an abridgement. The third makes the word edition do a job it cannot do. The fourth mistakes a small private edition for a commercial calculation, which is the reading the press's own purpose contradicts.
questions.hint: Ask who reads a quarterly review, and what a reader may therefore expect to be needed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The notes at the end of The Waste Land
questions.learningObjective: identify what a poem's apparatus is doing to a reader
questions.stem: The Waste Land ends with a short set of notes, fewer than the number of a reader might expect for a poem that quotes and paraphrases several languages and traditions, and the poem's text itself contains a place where a sentence is printed in capitals to mark a voice. What is the arrangement doing?

options.text: It relieves the reader, since any apparatus at all is a promise that nothing will be left unexplained
options.misconception: treats a partial apparatus as a complete promise, which is the opposite of what a few notes do

options.text: It shifts the burden to the critic, since once a poem has notes the job of reading becomes scholarly work and the poem is only the pretext
options.misconception: makes apparatus transfer all the work to criticism, which is a claim about criticism rather than about notes

options.text: It dates the poem, since a note that identifies a source is a date and a set of dates is a chronology
options.misconception: treats a note as a date, when a note identifies a source and says nothing about when the poem was written

options.text: It makes the poem's difficulty a visible, chosen object rather than a failure, since a reader is shown exactly where help is being withheld and where it is being offered

questions.explanation: The arrangement is editorial in the strong sense: it decides what a reader is left to do. A few notes say here is help, here is a source identified, here is a line printed in capitals for a reason, and everywhere else the reader is on their own with a poem that is quoting without announcing. That is a different experience from a poem that explains itself throughout, and it is the experience the poem is built to produce; the notes are the argument's boundary, and crossing it changes the reader. The capitals are the same device in miniature, a place where the typography itself says a voice has entered. A reader who wants the poem to be easier should notice that the notes do not try to make it easier; they make the difficulty exact. The second option mistakes an apparatus for a promise of completeness, which is the reading a reader brings to a schoolroom gloss. The third and fourth both assign to the apparatus a job it is not doing.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is being shown as well as what is being withheld.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Auden's later revision of September 1, 1939
questions.learningObjective: read an author's reworking of his own poem as evidence about the poem
questions.stem: Auden's poem first printed as September 1, 1939 appeared in a weekly magazine in 1939, and in later printings he altered it, changing its epigraph and its closing stanza, and he said he no longer wished to be identified with the version as first published. What does that establish?

options.text: That the first version was a mistake, since an author's refusal to be associated with a text settles the question of its quality
options.misconception: turns a refusal of association into a verdict on the text's merit

options.text: That the poem has two states, and that a reader who quotes it must say which, because the changes are the author's judgment on the poem's occasion
That the later text is a different poem, since changing an epigraph and a stanza amounts to writing a new work under the same name
options.misconception: overstates the change, which is a revision rather than a replacement

options.text: That the poem cannot be dated, since a title naming a day in 1939 is contradicted by an author who later disowned it
options.misconception: uses an author's later attitude to overturn a title-page date, which is not evidence about date

questions.explanation: A revision by the author is a rare piece of evidence and it should be used precisely. The changes are not a new poem: an epigraph sets a frame and a closing stanza sets a landing, and altering both alters what a reader is asked to do with the middle, which is where the poem's force is. The author's own statement, that he would not be associated with the earlier state, is a claim about the occasion rather than about the lines, and a reader who wants to understand why will look at the epigraph, since an epigraph is exactly where a poet says what the poem is for and to whom. The result is a poem with two states and a documented difference of intention, which is a gift to criticism rather than an embarrassment. The second option converts a change of mind into a verdict on quality, which no author has the standing to give after the fact. The third calls a revision a new work. The fourth lets an author's feeling override a date.
questions.hint: Ask what an epigraph does, and what changing it changes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Whitman's Song of Myself and its rearrangement across editions
questions.learningObjective: read a change in stanza arrangement as an editorial decision about a poem
questions.stem: Whit'sman's Song of Myself was twelve lines long in the 1855 edition of Leaves of Grass, and in later editions the poem was broken into shorter units and given a lineation and a set of breaks that the first printing did not have. What does the later arrangement do to a reader?

options.text: It corrects an error, since a poem printed without lineation was plainly waiting for a printer to supply the missing arrangement
options.misconception: assumes lineation is a mechanical supply, when it is an act of interpretation

options.text: It shortens the poem, since dividing a long poem into units makes the whole shorter to get through
options.misconception: confuses the length of the text with the length of the reading

options.text: It changes the rate at which the poem is read, since the new breaks put breaths where the first printing had none and the reader's own pace is thereby redirected
It makes the poem a song, since a poem divided into short printed units is a poem meant to be sung rather than read
options.misconception: infers a mode of performance from a typographic arrangement

questions.explanation: Lineation is the poet's decision about where a reader breathes, and it is one of the least visible and most consequential of them. The same words set as one long movement and set as a series of short units ask different things of a reader: one is a sentence that keeps going, the other is a sequence of arrivals. A poet who revisits his own work and adds breaks is making a claim about pace, and the claim is available to a reader who compares the two states, which is one of the more reliable things a reader can do with an author who revised. It is not a correction of a defect; the first state was a finished poem and it was printed as one. Nor is it a change of length, since the words are the words. And a typographic arrangement is not a musical instruction: a poem set in short printed units is still read, and a reader who cannot sing it has lost nothing that was there.
questions.hint: Ask where a reader breathes in each of the two states.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Raven's six stanzas and its refusal of revision
questions.learningObjective: read an author's claim about his own process as a position with consequences
questions.stem: Poe's The Raven, printed in 1845, is six stanzas of five lines with a three-line closing, and its metre is a trochaic line of eight syllables with the last one dropped. Poe also said the poem was not intended to be read as a poem and that he could not revise it. What is the reader being told?

options.text: That the poem is finished, so a reader who suggests a change is proposing to spoil a work the author has already declared complete
options.misconception: takes a rhetorical claim of unfinishability as a statement of completion

options.text: That the poem is an accident, since a writer who cannot revise has not decided what the poem is for
options.misconception: infers aimlessness from a claim about revision

options.text: That the poem should be read silently, since a poem its author calls a performance is not a poem to be read at all
options.misconception: turns a claim about reading into a prohibition on reading

options.text: That the poem is a performance of a voice rather than a composition, so the claim about revising is part of the effect and the dropping of the last syllable is what makes the voice keep going

questions.explanation: The claim is doing work inside the poem rather than describing a way of writing. A voice that keeps repeating itself and cannot be stopped is made audible by two things: the refrain, which the same five-beat line delivers over and over, and the dropped final syllable, which removes the beat's resolution and leaves the line arriving a fraction short every time. A reader who has the six stanzas in the ear has heard the voice circling, and a statement that the thing cannot be revised belongs to the same picture of a mind that cannot get free of what has happened to it. The line count supports the reading too: six stanzas of the same five lines with a short close is a shape that can go on, and the third stanza is where the words come back at their most insistent. The second option treats the claim as a completion guarantee, the third as an absence of intention, and the fourth as an instruction not to read, which is the opposite of what the sentence does.
questions.hint: Ask what the dropped syllable does to the beat at the end of each line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Gold-Bug in a weekly magazine and the prize it won
questions.learningObjective: read a magazine commission as evidence about the conditions of writing
questions.stem: Poe's The Gold-Bug was written for a competition in a Philadelphia newspaper, printed there in two instalments on 21 and 28 June 1843, and won a first premium of one hundred dollars, and it is a story of about four thousand words. What does that arrangement tell a reader about the shape of the story?

options.text: That the story is too long for a magazine, so the magazine must have printed it in parts and a reader with the parts has a better text
options.misconception: assumes a length constraint was broken and invents a serialisation

options.text: That the story was built to a length set by someone else, so its divisions are the shape of a single instalment and a reader should look for what that length makes easy
That the prize required a particular subject, since prizes are always given for a theme and the gold of the title is therefore the theme
options.misconception: infers a prescribed subject from a length requirement

options.text: That the story was written after the prize was offered, since a writer who composes to a length does not find a length afterwards
options.misconception: insists on a sequence the record does not fix

questions.explanation: A commission with a stated length is a formal instruction, and the effect of such an instruction is strongest on the joints of a text rather than on its content. A newspaper that pays a premium and prints a winner in instalments has asked for a story that will hold a reader from one week to the next, and the constraint that produces is a demand for a shape rather than a subject. Few characters who need introducing, one situation rather than several, and a movement that can be carried across a column and resumed in the next one, because a reader who has finished a column must find something that makes the next one worth buying. That is exactly the architecture of this story, and it is a reason to read its divisions as decisions rather than as arbitrary breaks. The length also tells a reader something about the newspaper's readership and about the economics of the form, which is why a four-thousand-word novella in a weekly paper is a fact worth more than the word novella usually carries. The second option invents a serialisation and calls the longer text a better one. The third confuses a length with a subject. The fourth settles a sequence the record does not.
questions.hint: Ask what a single instalment of one page makes easy to organise.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dickinson's fascicles as hand-sewn booklets
questions.learningObjective: read a surviving artefact as a claim about how a body of work was meant to be held
questions.stem: A large part of Emily Dickinson's poetry survives in about forty small booklets that she folded, pierced and sewn herself, in which the poems are printed in a fixed order and often carry alternative words in the margin. What does the object tell a reader that a printed collection cannot?

options.text: That the poems are unfinished, since a hand-sewn booklet has no publisher and no printer to have imposed a final form
options.misconception: assumes no publisher means no completion, which is an argument from circumstance

options.text: That the poems are private, since a booklet sewn at home was clearly intended for nobody, which makes the poems in a periodical later a different text
options.misconception: concludes privacy from the object's place of making, which is not a consequence

options.text: That the order of the poems and the state of the wording were settled by the poet, and that a later editor who rearranges or picks a reading has changed something the poet decided
That the collection is a sequence, since sewing poems in a fixed order is the same as writing them in that order, and readers should read them as a sequence
options.misconception: conflates the order of a booklet with the order of composition or of reading

questions.explanation: The fascicle is evidence about editorial authority, and that is why it has been argued over. In a sewn booklet the poet chose the sequence, the spacing and, in a great many cases, the alternative word in the margin; the object itself therefore contains decisions that a printed edition can only report. A reader who reorders those poems, or who prints one reading and deletes the alternative, has made a change the poet's own arrangement makes unnecessary, and can no longer claim to have found the order rather than supplied it. That is a genuine difficulty for every edition, and it is why editors differ about whether chronological or fascicle order should govern, since both are orderings the poet did not choose. The second option argues from circumstance to quality of finish, the third from a place of making to an intention, and the fourth from a place in a booklet to a place in a history.
questions.hint: Ask what the booklet decides that a printed page can only report.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dickinson's dashes and capital letters as editorial problems
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a marker's grammar from a marker's noise
questions.stem: Editors of Dickinson's poems have had to decide whether the dashes she used instead of commas and full stops are pauses, breaks in the syntax, or simply a way of writing when there was no paper, and whether her capitalising of common nouns is emphasis or the ordinary habit of a hand trained in an earlier century. What follows?

options.text: That the marks are noise, so a modern edition should regularise them and a reader will lose nothing that the poet intended
options.misconception: dismisses the marks as scribal accident without argument

options.text: That the capitals prove the poems were written to be read aloud, since a reader listening would need the initial letter of a noun emphasised
options.misconception: infers a mode of performance from a typographic habit

options.text: That the manuscripts are too uncertain to edit, so the poems should be published in the order in which the paper happened to survive
options.misconception: concludes from difficulty of editing to a rule about sequence

options.text: That an editor has to argue about the marks before the poem can be punctuated, and that a uniform modern punctuation is a decision taken on the poet's behalf and should be declared

questions.explanation: Punctuation is grammar, and where a text's grammar is in question the edition has to argue before it can tidy. If a dash is a pause, the poem's sentences are longer than a modern reader will assume; if it is a break in the syntax, they are shorter and the fragments are intentional; if it is a writing habit, it carries no grammatical weight at all, and a reader who regularises the marks has imposed sentences the poet never wrote. The capitals raise the same question on the other side, since a capital on a common noun can be emphasis or can be the ordinary practice of a hand that was taught differently. The honest editorial position is to argue, to choose, and to declare the choice, because a uniform modern punctuation is never neutral. The second option dismisses the marks without argument, the third reads a hand's habit as an instruction to a performer, and the fourth lets one problem swallow a decision about a different one.
questions.hint: Ask what a modern reader inherits when a text's punctuation is regularised.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Alice in 1865 and the author's name withdrawn from the title page
questions.learningObjective: read a change in a title page as a decision about how a book will be received
questions.stem: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland was published by a London firm in 1865 in an edition of about two thousand copies, and after publication the author's pseudonym was removed from the title page, so the copies of the first issue and the later issues differ. What does the difference do to a bibliographer?

options.text: It makes the first issue a distinct object, since a copy with the name and a copy without it are not the same bibliographical entity and must be described differently
It means the first issue is a different book, since a title page naming an author and a title page naming nobody are different books by definition
options.misconception: collapses a bibliographical state into a different work, which is a much stronger claim than the evidence allows

options.text: It shows the book was written by two people, since a pseudonym withdrawn at this stage implies a second author took over the name
options.misconception: reads a change of imprint as a change of authorship

options.text: It makes the later issue the correct text, since an author who has removed his name has thereby indicated which printing he wants remembered
options.misconception: treats a decision about a title page as a decision about a text

questions.explanation: Bibliographical states are exactly this: the same work, materially different, and a catalogue has to be able to tell a collector which is in front of it. A title page is part of the book's evidence, and a name appearing on one printing and not another is a difference that gets recorded, priced and described, because it marks a decision made at a particular moment. It is a small fact and it is worth a great deal, since it puts a date on a change of heart about how the book should present itself, at a time when a pseudonym on a title page was a much larger decision than it later became. What it does not do is create a second book, a second author or a different text, and it certainly does not make the later printing more correct. The second option overstates by a whole category, the third invents a second writer, and the fourth turns a marketing decision into an author's instruction about which text to read.
questions.hint: Ask what a collector needs to record about two copies of one book.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Christabel and its lines of four stresses
questions.learningObjective: read a metrical experiment as a claim about the kind of story a poem can tell
questions.stem: Coleridge's Christabel, composed in 1799 and 1800 and printed in 1816, is in lines that carry four stresses and vary in their number of syllables, and the story is carried by two speakers whose different voices are the point of the poem. What do the two decisions have in common?

options.text: That both give the reader a second thing to attend to at once, so that a line's beat and a voice's tone carry separate information in the same breath
That both are consequences of the poem's subject matter, since a story about a second voice must be in a flexible metre
options.misconception: makes a formal decision a consequence of plot, when the two are independent choices

options.text: That both make the poem harder to read on purpose, since difficulty is the price a poem pays for originality
options.misconception: offers a motive that fits any innovation and therefore explains nothing

options.text: That both were attempts to write in a foreign language, since a metre with four beats is the metre of many tongues rather than of English
options.misconception: derives a metrical choice from a claim about translation

questions.explanation: The two decisions are parallel because each of them gives the poem a second channel. The four-stress line with a variable count of syllables means the reader's ear is following a beat that does not fit the sentence exactly, so the line is saying something on its own account, and the effect is a kind of muscular insistence independent of the sense. The second voice does the same thing in a different register: a reader has to hold two tones at once and decide which one the poem is trusting. A poem about enchantment and interruption is well served by a form that will not settle, and a reader who has met the two speakers in the poem will recognise the arrangement as one decision made twice. The second option makes the metre a consequence of plot, which reverses the relation. The third is a motive that would explain any innovation and so explains none. The fourth mistranslates a metrical fact into a claim about languages.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is being asked to follow at the same time.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A passage in four-stress lines and what it shares with Hopkins
questions.learningObjective: recognise a metrical principle in a passage written for the question

stimulus.body: an original passage written for this question in a four-stress, ten-syllable line
stimulus.license: original text written for this question; no protected text used

questions.stem: A passage written for this question in the manner Hopkins used runs: "The chapel bell is struck by nobody / And candle-wax has gathered on the stair / Where forty winters of the choirmen were." Each line is checked in two ways. What does the check find?

options.text: Four stresses and ten syllables in every line, and the difference from Hopkins is that Hopkins allowed the syllable count to move while a line of ten syllables fixes it
Four stresses in every line and ten syllables in every line, so the regularity is exact on both counts and nothing is irregular
options.misconception: mistakes a coincidental agreement for the principle Hopkins is after, which is that only the stresses are regular

options.text: Ten syllables in every line but a varying number of stresses, so the regularity is in the count and the variety in the beat
options.misconception: inverts the two counts, which is the standard error about stress metrics

options.text: An irregular count of both stresses and syllables, since a line ending on a monosyllable cannot be made to carry a fixed number of beats
options.misconception: supposes a line's last word disturbs its stress count, which is a misreading of how beats are counted

questions.explanation: The check has to be made on both counts separately, because the principle depends on which of them is allowed to move. In this passage both come out at four and ten for every line, so it is a regular line and nothing about it demonstrates the principle. Hopkins's practice keeps the stresses at four and lets the syllables vary, which is what makes the ear count beats and stop counting syllables; a writer who fixes the syllable count at ten is working inside a different and older convention, in which the line length is the rule and the stresses are fitted to it. Both kinds of line can be good, and the difference is a difference about what a reader should trust. The first option calls the agreement exact on both counts and misses that the counts need not agree. The second reverses them. The fourth invents a difficulty at the line ending, which is where a beat is most predictable.
questions.hint: Count the stresses and count the syllables, and then ask which one Hopkins fixes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An unrhymed tercet and what marks the end of its unit
questions.learningObjective: diagnose what carries a reader through verse that rhymes with nothing

stimulus.body: an original passage written for this question in an unrhymed five-foot line
stimulus.license: original text written for this question; no protected text used

questions.stem: A passage written for this question in the manner Swinburne used in Ave at que Vale runs: "The years go by like water on a stone / And I have said the sorrow that is mine / Shall outlast marble, and outlast the tomb." What marks the joint between the three lines for a reader?

options.text: The completion of the sense, since the sentence is continuous through the first two lines and the third closes it, so the reading breath falls where the grammar falls
The length of the lines, since lines of five feet are long enough that a reader must pause at the end of each one whatever the sense is doing
options.misconception: makes a line length produce a pause regardless of sense, which is the opposite of what length does

options.text: The stanza, since the three lines are printed together and a reader has been trained to pause at the end of a printed unit
options.misconception: attributes the pause to a printed boundary rather than to the sense

options.text: Nothing, since verse without rhyme gives a reader no signal at all and the passage must be read as an undifferentiated block
options.misconception: claims that unrhymed verse gives no signal, which is contradicted by the sense the passage completes

questions.explanation: The joint is audible because of the grammar, and the passage is built to make that obvious. The first two lines run on: the subject of the sentence is separated from its verb by a completed subordinate clause, so a reader arrives at the end of the second line still inside the sentence and does not pause there. The third line carries the verb and the object and stops, so the breath falls exactly where the sentence does. That is the whole mechanism by which verse without rhyme holds its units together, and it is why an unrhymed line is harder to write than a rhymed one: nothing will rescue a line whose sense has not arrived at an end. Line length as such does nothing, since a long line whose sense runs on is harder to leave than a short one. Nor is a stanza a sufficient signal; readers have learned to read across stanzas, and a printed break is not a grammatical event. The second and fourth options both claim a mechanism that the passage does not use.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence ends at the end of the second line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A bibliography of one poem in the order the evidence arrived
questions.learningObjective: order the physical evidence by which state of a text it establishes
questions.stem: Four witnesses to the same poem have been printed out of order. Place them in the order a reader must establish them, given that each answers a different question about the text's history.

options.text: a letter in which the poet quotes two lines to a friend, which is the earliest evidence that the lines existed at all
a typescript sent to a typesetter, which fixes the wording that was set up for printing
a magazine printing, which gives the poem its first public text and therefore the form most readers meet
an annotated edition of seventy years later, which records variants and adds readings the earlier witnesses do not carry

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by what each witness can settle. A quotation in a letter establishes the earliest point at which the lines are known to have existed, which is prior to any printing decision and cannot be recovered from the printings. The typescript settles what was actually set up, which is a different question from what the poet wrote and a different one again from what the magazine printed, and it comes before the printing in the chain of evidence. The magazine printing then gives the text its first public existence, and it is the state most readers will encounter, which is why a reader who wants to know what a poem has been treated as should start there and work backwards. The annotated edition is last because it is downstream of everything: it can only report variants it has found in the earlier witnesses and can add nothing the earlier witnesses do not contain. The order cannot be reversed, because each step's authority depends on the steps before it.
questions.hint: Ask which witness settles the earliest question and which settles the latest.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two ways of making a long meditation hold its shape
questions.learningObjective: compare two formal solutions to the same structural problem
questions.stem: Two long meditations of the nineteenth century solve the same structural problem in opposite ways. In one, the fourth and fifth lines of each stanza make a pair whose second member stands alone and answers the first with a near-rhyme; in the other, each stanza of eight lines is half long quatrain and half short quatrain. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: Both poems solve the problem of sustaining attention in a long meditation, one by refusing to let a stanza close and the other by letting a stanza close twice at two different weights
Both poems are songs of fixed form, since a set number of stanzas and a set number of lines per stanza make both works closed forms in the same sense
options.misconception: calls both closed forms, which ignores the difference between a stanza count and a stanza pattern

options.text: Only the second poem is a long meditation, since five stanzas cannot sustain an argument and a poem of more than a hundred stanzas is a meditation by definition
options.misconception: judges a poem's length by its kind, which mistakes a scale for a genre

options.text: The first poem is metrically irregular and the second metrically regular, so the two poems solve their problems in opposite ways and nothing connects them
options.misconception: reduces two formal decisions to regularity and irregularity, which misses what each is for

questions.explanation: Both poems face the same difficulty and both answer it at the level of stanza rather than of theme. A meditation that runs long has to give the reader repeated small completions without exhausting itself. Keats's ode gives five units of ten lines in which the fifth line is set apart and does not fully answer the fourth, so the reader gets an almost-closure five times and is never allowed to rest; the argument is conducted inside a form that keeps withdrawing its own conclusion. In Memoriam gives a unit in which a long quatrain states something at length and a short quatrain registers the recoil, and the reader is given a full stop roughly every eight lines for more than a hundred repetitions. One form refuses the closure, the other supplies it twice at two weights, and both are answers to the same problem of sustaining attention. The second option makes a stanza count a closed form, the third judges by length, and the fourth reduces two different decisions to the same axis of regularity.
questions.hint: Ask where each poem gives its reader a small completion.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a bibliographer can and cannot establish about a date
questions.learningObjective: state the limits of a method rather than only its results
questions.stem: A poet's poem was first printed in a weekly magazine, a draft exists in a friend's hand, a manuscript carries a year that has been struck out, and a collected edition prints a third version. Explain what can be established about the poem's history from this evidence, and what cannot.

answer.exemplar: Four kinds of evidence are present and they answer four different questions, so the first job is to sort them. The magazine printing fixes a public existence: a dated issue of a named periodical is a fact anyone can look up. The typescript fixes what was set up for printing, which is neither what the poet wrote nor what the magazine printed. The struck-out year is evidence about revision rather than composition, and its force is that somebody changed it. The collected edition is downstream of everything and can add readings the earlier witnesses do not carry. What cannot be established: the moment of composition; whether the first printed text is the earliest form of the words; and which reading the poet would have chosen, since an alternative word in a margin is an acknowledged uncertainty. A good answer also says what would settle each question: a dated letter quoting the lines, a second typescript, an authors marked copy. The mistake to avoid is presenting a chain of witnesses as if it were a chain of composition.

questions.explanation: The useful shape of an answer here is a list of witnesses, a list of questions, and then a line drawn between what the witnesses settle and what they do not. The first job is to keep the four kinds of evidence apart, because they are routinely confused and the confusion is what produces false dates. A dated printing is a public fact; a setting document is a private fact about what was meant for the press; a manuscript is evidence about revision; a collected edition is a comparison. Sorting them is most of the work, and the reward is that each question gets an answer of the right kind: the printing is checkable by looking, the manuscript is checkable by inspecting, and the collected edition is checkable only against the others. A good answer then says plainly what the sorting does not buy, which is the moment of composition and the poet's final preference among variant readings, and it should note what would settle each: a dated letter, a second setting document, an author's marked copy. The failure to avoid is presenting a chain of witnesses as though it were a chain of composition; a reader who does that will end up dating a poem by the date of the latest edition.
questions.hint: Separate the printing date, the setting date, the manuscript evidence and the later editorial text, and say which of them can be checked by looking.
